text: It is just after dawn on 1 December 1948. On Somerton Beach, Adelaide, a man is found sitting against the sea wall.
Dead.
He is well dressed. His shoes are polished. And there is not a single label on his clothes.
In his pockets: no wallet. No identification. No name.
He would become Australia's most profound mystery. The Somerton Man.
This is that file, read out one exhibit at a time.
What the evidence proves. What it does not. And the name science attached to the man on the beach, 74 years later.
The body was found at 6:30 am, on the sand at Somerton Park, opposite the Crippled Children's Home.
Lying back against the sea wall, legs extended, feet crossed — a half-smoked cigarette on his right collar.
Pathologist John Burton Cleland: a man in top physical condition.
About 40–45. 180 cm. Grey eyes. Fair to ginger hair, greying at the temples.
Hands with no sign of manual labour.
Toes that met in a wedge — like a dancer, or a man used to pointed boots.
White shirt. Red, white and blue tie. Brown knitted pullover.
A double-breasted jacket of apparently American tailoring.
Every label removed. No hat — unusual in 1948.
No wallet. Clean-shaven. No identification of any kind.
Pockets: an unused rail ticket to Henley Beach.
A bus ticket. A US-made comb. Half-empty Juicy Fruit gum.
An Army Club packet holding 7 Kensitas cigarettes. A quarter-full box of matches.
At 7 pm the night before, a couple watched him extend his right arm to its fullest extent — and drop it.
Limply.
Motionless for half an hour. It struck them as odd that he never once swatted at the mosquitoes.
Drunk, they assumed. Or asleep.
The autopsy: organs congested, spleen three times normal
size, blood mixed with food in the stomach. And no foreign substance — none — was ever found.
"I am quite convinced the death could not have been natural." — pathologist John Dwyer.
Poison, invisible to every test 1948 could run.
June 1949, around the inquest: police re-examine the dead man's clothing.
Sewn inside a trouser pocket: a concealed fob pocket. Rolled inside it — a tiny scrap of paper.
Two printed words. Tamám Shud. Persian. It means: ended. It is finished.
The final words of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
— a book whose promise is to live fully, and end without regret.
Police released the photograph. Somewhere in Australia was the book it was torn from — a copy whose last page had a blank reverse.
22 July 1949: a man comes forward. In the back of his unlocked car, on Jetty Road, Glenelg — a copy of the Rubaiyat.
Police shielded him with a false name: Ronald Francis.
His real name has never been officially established.
The scrap matched the torn page. This was the book.
But its timing is disputed to this day — a week or two before the body? Or just after?
And then, on the inside back cover, the case changed shape entirely.
A 1941 edition of Edward FitzGerald's translation, published by Whitcombe and Tombs, Christchurch, New Zealand.
Under ultraviolet light, indentations rise from the inside back cover
— writing from the page above, carried through.
A local telephone number. A second, unidentified number.
And five lines of capital letters that looked like a code.
49 letters in five groups. The second line struck out — as if the writer had erred and begun again.
And a single X, above the end of another line.
The number belonged to a young nurse on Moseley
Street, Glenelg — 400 metres from where the body lay. Jessica Thomson.
She said she did not know the dead man. She recalled only that in late
1948, an unknown man had come asking about her at a neighbour's door.
Shown the plaster cast, she was — in Detective Sergeant Lionel Leane's words
— "completely taken aback, to the point of giving the appearance that she was about to faint."
She asked that her name be kept from the record.
Police agreed. It would hamper the case for decades.
1978: Defence cryptographers find too few symbols for any meaningful answer.
The letters might even be the "meaningless" product of a disturbed mind.
2004: detective Gerry Feltus reads the last line as "It's Time To Move To South Australia
— Moseley Street." 2014: the letters match initials of English text
— but no text on earth matches them.
The original book was lost in the 1950s. The code has never been broken.
14 January 1949: an unclaimed brown suitcase, checked into the Adelaide station cloakroom after 11 am on 30 November
— the day before the death.
Inside: a dressing gown, slippers, underpants,
pyjamas, shaving things — and trousers with sand in the cuffs.
An electrician's screwdriver. A table knife cut down into a short, sharp instrument.
Scissors with sharpened points. A square of zinc — perhaps a sheath.
A stencilling brush of the kind used aboard merchant ships.
A card of Barbour orange waxed thread — a type not sold in Australia.
The same thread had repaired the pocket of the trousers he was wearing.
Again, the labels were gone. This time, three had been missed: a tie marked T.
Keane. A laundry bag marked Keane. A singlet marked Kean.
No T. Keane was missing in any English-speaking country.
The dry-cleaning marks in the clothes led nowhere.
Police believed he arrived by overnight train — Melbourne, Sydney, or Port Augusta.
He bought a ticket for the 10:50 am train to Henley Beach — and never boarded it.
He checked the suitcase. He caught a bus to Glenelg.
And the last day of his life dissolves into an ordinary street map.
In 1986, the suitcase and everything in it was destroyed.
The objects are gone. Only photographs and lists remain.
Nothing in that case explained who he was. Everything in it seemed designed to say less, not more.
A body without a name invites theories. Separate them from the evidence, and the case becomes clearer — by becoming smaller.
Theory: espionage. A secret code. An undetectable poison.
The Cold War overhead. A seductive story — and nothing in the file supports it.
Theory: suicide. The Rubaiyat's promise — to end without regret.
Police suspected it; at the inquest they gave the paper no
significance, and no evidence corroborated it.
Theory: the body was brought to the beach. The shoes were "remarkably clean" for a man said to have wandered Glenelg all day.
Poison usually kills with vomiting and convulsions — there was none.
Cleland allowed it — and stressed: speculation.
The name Keane. The American tailoring. The stencilling brush.
Each has fed a theory of hidden identity. None survives contact with the file.
1959: a witness reports he and three others saw a well-dressed man carrying another man on his shoulders along the
beach, the night before. Never corroborated.
As one journalist wrote in 1949: the Somerton Man "made certain that the glass would be
empty, save for speculation."
2009: a University of Adelaide team led by Derek Abbott takes up the case
— and finds the autopsy reports themselves have vanished from the record.
Two anatomical rarities: an unusually formed ear.
And hypodontia — missing lateral incisors. Each in only 1–2 people in a hundred.
In the plaster death cast of 1949, strands of the man's own hair had been sealed beneath the surface — preserved for 70 years.
February 2018: mitochondrial DNA read — a lineage carried by about 1% of Europeans.
Not enough. mtDNA follows only the mother's line.
May 2021: the body is exhumed from West Terrace Cemetery
— where it had rested under a marker: "Here lies the unknown man who was found at Somerton Beach."
26 July 2022: Abbott and forensic genealogist Colleen Fitzpatrick announce a name
— built from those hairs in the death mask. Genealogical matches on both sides of a family tree.
CARL “CHARLES” WEBB · born 16 November 1905,
Footscray, Melbourne · electrical engineer and instrument maker.
Webb had lost four close relatives in 7 years.
His marriage to Dorothy Robertson had collapsed
— she described a solitary, moody man, fond of poetry. Poems, she said, mostly about death.
A sister named Keane, and a brother-in-law who had travelled through the US
— could explain the American clothes, and the tags that misled police for 70 years.
South Australia Police and Forensic Science SA have not verified the identification.
They were "cautiously optimistic." The name rests on the strongest genetic case yet assembled
— and remains, formally, a claim.
What the file proves: a man died on Somerton Beach, 1 December 1948.
He went to great lengths to erase his name. He carried the end of a poem.
Science has given him a probable name — Carl Webb
— while the authorities stop short of confirming it.
Three things still do not fit: the polished shoes.
The absence of vomiting. The unused ticket. Each is evidence of something. We do not know of what.
The cause of death was never determined. The code was never broken.
Everything else — the spies, the secrets, the romance — remains what it always was.
Story, waiting for proof.
The file goes back in the drawer, among others like it. But the drawer does not close the case.
On a grave in West Terrace Cemetery, the words still stand: "Here lies the unknown man who was found at Somerton Beach."
The evidence is real. The name is new. The answer is still missing.
